title: When Did Oklahoma Switch to the Wishbone? The 1970 Gamble
question: When did Oklahoma switch to the wishbone offense, and who made the call?
answer: Oklahoma switched to the wishbone midway through the 1970 season under head coach Chuck Fairbanks, debuting it against Texas on Oct. 10, 1970. Offensive coordinator Barry Switzer persuaded Fairbanks to make the change after an early loss to Oregon State.
summary: OU switched to the wishbone in October 1970 under Chuck Fairbanks, debuting it against Texas after Barry Switzer pushed for the change. Here is how.
body: The offense that defined Oklahoma football for a generation started as a midseason gamble. Chuck Fairbanks had taken over in April 1967, promoted at age 33 after head coach Jim Mackenzie died suddenly, and he quickly won Big Eight titles in 1967 and 1968. By 1970, though, the Sooners were searching for answers.

Oklahoma opened the 1970 season in the I formation. After a third-game loss to Oregon State, offensive coordinator Barry Switzer convinced Fairbanks to scrap it and install the wishbone, the triple-option set Texas had been using, during an open week. The new look debuted in the Red River game in Dallas on Oct. 10, 1970, and it did not go well at first: Texas won 41-9.

The Sooners stuck with it. They won five of their last seven regular-season games, including a 66-6 rout of Oklahoma State, then tied Alabama 24-24 in the Astro-Bluebonnet Bowl in Houston on Dec. 31, 1970. By 1971, the Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History notes, OU was statistically the best team in college football.

Fairbanks won one more Big Eight title in 1972, then left in January 1973 to coach the NFL's New England Patriots. Switzer, the coordinator who had lobbied for the wishbone, was named his successor that same month and rode the offense to some of the best seasons in school history.
